title: Pressure-cooker butter chicken
subtitle: Creamy, mildly spiced, and ready in 20 minutes
excerpt: Tender chicken in a silky tomato and cream sauce cooked under pressure. The sauce is mellow and rich, a dish that suits everyone at the table, including those who find heat a challenge.
sourceNotes: Butter chicken (murgh makhani) was created at Moti Mahal restaurant in Delhi in the 1950s by Kundan Lal Gujral and popularised by Kundan Lal Jaggi. The dish uses a tomato-cream sauce to mellow leftover tandoor chicken. The home-kitchen adaptation uses standard chicken and the pressure cooker in place of a tandoor.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze before adding the cream. Add fresh cream after reheating. Keeps for up to 4 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily. Freeze without the cream.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the base up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate. Reheat and stir in the cream just before serving.

content.text: Butter chicken is one of the mildest and most widely enjoyed Indian-origin dishes in British cooking. The sauce is tomato-based, enriched with butter and cream, and mellowed by a short list of warm spices, it has heat from the chilli, but not the kind that overwhelms. The pressure cooker version cooks the sauce and chicken together in 12 minutes under pressure.

The butter is added in two stages: a small knob at the start to build the base, and a larger one stirred through at the end. This second addition is what gives the sauce its characteristic richness and gloss. Do not skip it.
Serve with basmati rice or naan. A spoonful of plain yoghurt over each portion cuts the richness if the sauce is very creamy.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Melt 20 g of the butter over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic and ginger; cook for 1 minute. Add the cumin, coriander, turmeric, and chilli powder; stir for 1 minute. Add the tomato puree and stir for 1 minute until darkened.
Add the chicken and stir to coat. Pour in the tinned tomatoes. Season with salt. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 12 minutes, then quick-release.

Open the lid. Stir in the remaining 40 g of butter in pieces until melted. Stir in {{double-cream}} of double cream and the garam masala. Simmer gently in the open pot for 3 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

rows.symptom: The sauce splits after adding the cream
rows.cause: The sauce was too hot when the cream went in, causing the fat to separate.
rows.fix: Let the pot cool for 2 minutes before adding the cream, and add it off direct heat, stirring gently.
Balance with a squeeze of lemon juice or a pinch of chilli powder.

rows.cause: The onion base was not cooked long enough, or the spices did not bloom.
rows.fix: The base needs a full 8 to 10 minutes of cooking before spices go in. Quick-cooked onion gives a flat, raw sauce. There is no shortcut for this step.

content.text: Cook the dish up to the point of adding the cream. Refrigerate for up to 2 days or freeze for up to 4 months. When reheating, bring to a simmer and stir in the cream and remaining butter fresh. This produces a better texture than freezing the cream.

Butter chicken became one of the most popular dishes in British Indian restaurants and, from there, crossed into regular home cooking. Its approachability, mild heat, rich sauce, tender meat, makes it a gateway dish for families with varied heat tolerances. The pressure cooker version keeps the result reliable without requiring a long simmer or specialist technique.
